13.0.s.en: 1. Between deification and admiration of the Creator

13.0.0.en: 23 Therefore the hypocrites who lived in foolishness, You tormented with their own abominations. 24 For they went astray farther than the ways of error, having taken as gods those creatures that their enemies despise, deceived like children who have no understanding. 25 Therefore You sent upon them, as upon children without reason, a judgment to mock them. 26 But they that would not be admonished by the correction of mockery shall feel a judgment worthy of God. 27 For when they suffered in their indignation, and saw that those whom they had taken to be gods were the means of their torment, they acknowledged the true God, whom they had formerly denied to know; and therefore the end of condemnation came upon them.

13.0.1.en: Surely all men who are ignorant of God are naturally vain, for they were not able to know Him who is from the good things that are seen, nor did they recognize the Maker by considering His works. [1]

13.0.2.en: Man did not know the explanation of natural phenomena: the power of the sun to give light, to warm and to purify, and to determine day and night; the power of fire to consume; the lightning that appears for moments and disappears, so that he supposed that the god was angry with men, and so on. All this led some to set up these powers and phenomena as gods. God warned His people against following the pagans in this matter: “Lest you lift up your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, should be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the Lord your God has divided unto all nations under the whole heaven” (Deut 4:19).

13.0.3.en: Because man fell into this worship, the hymn of the Three Young Men in the fiery furnace came to deal with this matter, in which man offers praise to God, calling all creation to worship God with him.

13.0.4.en: “O all you works of the Lord, bless the Lord; praise Him and exalt Him above all for ever... O you heavens, bless the Lord... angels... sun and moon and stars... showers and dew... clouds and winds... fire and heat, etc.”

13.0.5.en: If man is amazed at the beauty and power of creation, it is fitting for him to praise its Creator, who showed such wonder in creating it for the sake of man.

13.0.6.en: Foolish are all men who fail to know God through their study of His works, considering His works themselves to be gods. Truly His works are great and glorious, but there is no ground for comparison between them and their Maker. The author did not offer rational or philosophical proofs of the existence of God, for it is a reality that is not a matter of discussion and debate, but a matter of experience and life.

13.0.7.en: In ignorance man put the beauty and power of the creatures in the place of the creativity of the Creator and His infinite power.

13.0.8.en: God speaks with mankind through His creation. As St. Paul says: “For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). And David the prophet says: “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament shows His handywork” (Ps 19:1). Pope Athanasius the Apostolic wrote: [By His Word (the Logos) God gave the world to be, so that men might be able to know Him through His works, He who by nature is invisible; for the artist, though he is not seen, is known by his works.]

13.0.9.en: * Creation itself, by its harmony and order, proclaims the greatness of the divine nature.

13.0.10.en: Father John of Damascus * How did God reveal Himself? By a voice from heaven? Not at all! God made a throne of splendor able to draw men more than a voice. He set before them the enormous creation, so that the wise and the unlearned, the Scythians and the barbarians, might ascend to God, learning through the sight of the beauty of the things they see.

13.0.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * It is fitting for all who live on this earth to begin by using the senses upon sensible things, that they may pass from them to the knowledge of intelligible things. But their knowledge must not stop at sensible things.

13.0.12.en: Origen * In all visible things clear reminders of the Maker of good things take hold of us. So we give no opportunity to sins, and leave no place in our hearts for the enemy, if we have God dwelling in us through our constant remembrance of Him.

13.0.13.en: St. Basil the Great * It is very easy to understand that the Creator of the angels, principalities and powers is He who in a moment of His power made all this great beauty of the world out of nothing, when it had no existence, and gave being to things and causes that did not exist.

13.0.14.en: St. Ambrose * The prophet also said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps 19:1). Will the pagans say at the judgment that they were ignorant of the existence of God? Did they not hear the heavens sending forth a voice through the harmony of the order of all things, speaking plainly as with a trumpet? Did you not see the hours of the night and the day remaining unchanged, and the good order of winter and spring and the other seasons standing firm and unmoved...? Yet God did not make this great order so in order to teach the pagans so that they might be without excuse, but He set it forth that they might come to know Him. But by failing to recognize Him they deprive themselves of any excuse.

13.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom But they deemed either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the violent water, or the lights of heaven, to be the gods which govern the world. [2]

13.1.1.en: What concerns the author is not only that God is Creator, but that being the Creator He cares for His creation. Life does not proceed by chance nor by an inevitable fate, as many of the philosophers and astrologers thought; some suppose that the spheres or other things govern the world by an unavoidable decree, but God in His fatherhood watches over the world and cares for it.

13.1.2.en: * The pagans tried to reach heaven, but since they shattered the light that was in them, and instead committed themselves to the darkness of their own minds, they sought the immaterial in bodies, and the unlimited in created forms, and by this they lost their harmony with the light.

13.1.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * Moses began to speak, saying: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). After that the teacher began to record what happened in the six days of the creative power. By prophecy of lofty vision he beheld the Hidden One calling what was nothing to rise and become something; and the signs and the voices that were directed to the creatures, Moses heard and saw by the light of prophecy. He had entered into the treasury of divinity like a steward, and the riches of the creative power were not hidden from him; and as he saw and as he heard in the exalted place, so the teacher who preaches concerning the creatures set it down in his book.

13.1.4.en: He said: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, and proved that the world has an origin and a beginning. From Mount Sinai Moses brought down to the world, which had been darkened by idolatry, a teaching full of light. When creatures of every shape were being worshipped, they were counted like gods in their natures; the world was darkened by the love of vain idols, creation forgot its Maker and He was no longer remembered, and men worshipped either fire, or water, or the stars, or animals, or birds.

13.2.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh If they supposed those to be gods because they were delighted with their beauty, let them know how much greater their Lord is than they, for He who created them is the source of beauty. [3]

13.2.1.en: Men were charmed by the beauty of creation and did not contemplate the love of the Creator. Therefore the Word of God, the Creator, came down to them, that by His practical love on the Cross He might draw them out of error and bring them into the divine truth.

13.2.2.en: * A cloud of errors covered their hearts. For while they ought to have honored the Creator of all through the beautiful creatures that He brought into being, they clung to what they had, saying that the things they were able to see were sufficient for their salvation.

13.2.3.en: Ambrosiaster * Your rays went forth to all quarters and gave them light, and behold, the peoples delight in Your light which has gladdened them; Your rays scattered all the darkness of idol worship and set up for You the image of light among those in darkness. You sent a message to the Magi by a star of light, and drew them and brought them out of darkness into Your light. Your messenger ran to preach to those in darkness, and prepared there the way for Your shining, that You might walk in it (Zech 6:12)...

13.2.4.en: He sent the light to kill the darkness in its place, and to make a path in the wilderness of idol worship. He cast a single ray of His lights upon the land, and by His shining scattered the strong night of error. He came to enlighten all the world by His birth, and first sent to the beginning of the earth (the Far East) that they might come to Him. He sent a messenger of light and preachers to the land far from teaching, to bring it so that it might be guided; He laid on the shoulder of the barbarians the yoke of the report, and set them on the road that they might come to His service...

13.2.5.en: The idols of Egypt saw the Savior and trembled and feared Him, as had been preached beforehand by prophecy (Isa 19:1)...

13.2.6.en: The pillars of Egypt that bore the idols all trembled before Him who came to break them by His crucifixion; all the platforms of sacrifices were destroyed by the high priest who came to the slaughter that He might abolish them. The Truth entered and whispered (in the ears of) the idols and terrified them, and called them to fall though they do not hear. Such things were said on the part of Justice to the idols of Egypt, rich in prostrations:

13.2.7.en: Fall down, you weak one; it is enough that you have conquered by metaphors. He to whom worship is due has come; leave Him the place that He may stand upon His kingdom. You dried husks, empty the place for the Son of God. You who were fashioned by error, come down from your palaces. You corrupt idols that have become snares for those who worship you, be broken and do not hunt any more for corruption. You weak one, flee from the Mighty One who has come to you, and stand no more in the place of the King who has arrived. You manufactured thing, you that took the name of God and troubled the earth, behold the Maker has come down from His place to put you to shame. The wind has gone out to gather the thorns from the fields; flee, you tares, from the tempest, the lady of the quarters. The host of idol worship feared the Mighty One, and the ranks of the idols were told the good news of their fall.

13.3.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh And if they were amazed at their power and working, let them understand from them how much more powerful is He who formed them. [4]

13.3.1.en: Man, fallen from his position, his dignity and his glory, loses the things that God gave him, and stands looking at nature and what is in it as though it were spirit; this has been called animism. So he worshipped stones, rivers and springs, as he worshipped trees and animals. In short, whenever he admired a power or a beauty or a particular trait in some being, he worshipped it. We mention by way of example:

13.3.2.en: The calf as a symbol of procreation.

13.3.3.en: The serpent as a symbol of the renewal of life, since it sheds its outer skin and a new skin takes its place, giving it vitality and energy.

13.3.4.en: The eagle and the falcon as a symbol of wisdom and of seeing from afar.

13.3.5.en: Natural phenomena such as storms, winds and fire as a symbol of the power that man cannot resist.

13.3.6.en: Sex and prostitution for the satisfaction of bodily lusts in unrestrained licentiousness.

13.3.7.en: Emperors, kings and heroes, even after their death.

13.3.8.en: Man often stands before nature amazed at its power and working, but it is fitting for him to realize the power of its wonderful Creator.

13.4.0.en: For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionally the Maker of them is seen. [5]

13.4.1.en: The greatness and beauty that characterize creation reveal the greatness of its Creator!

13.4.2.en: * “For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead” (Rom 1:20). What he means is this: He set His creation in the midst, before the eyes of men, that they might perceive the Creator from His works. Another writer pointed to the same: “For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionally (relatively) the Maker of them is seen” (Wis 13:5). Behold the greatness. Marvel at the power of its Maker! Do you see the beauty? Be amazed at the wisdom of its Creator! This is what the prophet meant when he said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps 19:1).

13.4.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * He Himself, being above all, the Ruler and King and Governor of power, does everything for the glory of His Father and for the knowledge of Him, so that even through the works themselves He teaches us.

13.4.4.en: * We learn from the creatures without asking voices from them, but as we hear the Holy Scriptures we believe, and by seeing the order of all things and their harmony we know that this is the Creator, Lord and God of all beings, and we perceive His astonishing providence and His sovereignty over all.

13.4.5.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * It is impossible for human eyes to see the divine nature, but they perceive its power to some extent through His divine works. Solomon says: “For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionally the Maker of them is seen.”

13.4.6.en: He did not say that the Creator is seen through His creation, but made clear that this is “proportionally,” for God is too great to be comprehended by any man through his beholding the greatness of creation. And as his heart is lifted up the more by beholding more (of the greatness of creation), he receives a greater knowledge of God.

13.4.7.en: * Refute those who blaspheme the wise and good Creator, and recognize from what you hear and read and discover that “from the greatness and beauty of creation its Maker is known proportionally.”

13.4.8.en: And as we bow our knees with good reverence before the Maker of the worlds, I mean the world of sense and the world of thought, what is seen and what is not seen, you glorify God with a holy tongue that murmurs of what is known, and lips that do not keep silent, and a heart that does not tire, saying: “How great are Your works, O Lord. In wisdom You have made them all”; honor and glory and majesty are due to You from now through all ages. Amen.

13.5.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Yet these men are less to be blamed, for they perhaps err only because they seek God and desire to find Him. [6]

13.5.1.en: Here the wise man has compassion on the pagans who were drawn to the greatness of creation, its power and its beauty, and at the beginning gave them a kind of excuse. Perhaps their aim was God Himself, and when they sought Him in creation they were dazzled by its beauty and turned aside from their goal.

13.5.2.en: The wise man went back to rebuke them, for though he gave them something of an excuse, he looks to what God gave them, namely the mind, which is able to pass beyond the limits of visible things to believe in Him who is invisible, if they had been sincere in seeking the truth.

13.6.0.en: For they search diligently among His works, and are persuaded by the sight, because the things that are seen are beautiful. [7]

13.6.1.en: Solomon, characterized by tenderness and compassion, again offered the pagans an excuse because of the attractive allurement of the beauty of creation.

13.7.0.en: Yet even they are not to be pardoned. [8]

13.7.1.en: As the wise man looks at the pagans who desire to find God and search for Him diligently, he excuses them to some extent; but when he finds them behaving without reason because of their attraction to temporal beauty and pleasures, he declares their condemnation and that there is no pardon for them as long as they do not return to Him.

13.8.0.en: For if they were able to know so much, that they could discern the essence of the world, how did they not more quickly find the Lord of it? [9]

13.8.1.en: What increases their responsibility in not knowing God is that they investigate the sciences of nature and perceive some of its secrets, whereas it was fitting for them to seek God, for knowing Him is quicker and easier than knowing the secrets of the universe.

13.8.2.en: God created man as lord of the earthly creation, and gave him a mind that he might come to know the secrets of the universe and enjoy knowledge.

13.8.3.en: Solomon the wise commends research in the sciences and the knowledge of the laws of nature, for God did not create the mind that we might bury it, but as a gift that we kindle for edification.

13.8.4.en: The matter does not stop at knowing the secrets of the universe, but the believer passes beyond nature, to enjoy the knowledge of heavenly things and taste the sweetness of their pledge, and experience fellowship with the Heavenly One, the Creator of heaven and earth.

13.8.5.en: The wise man grieves at the degradation to which man has come: instead of rising to heavenly things he sank down into pagan worship, which denies the true God and drives man to wallow in abominations, even to violence and the shedding of blood.

13.8.6.en: * In the hearts of the Gentiles the honor of the one purest God was changed into a bloody worship of various gods.

13.8.7.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * The world is beautiful without doubt, and lofty in the majesty of its size as in the order of its components, whether those in the oblique circle or those in the north or in its spherical shape. But it is not this but its Maker whom we must worship. If your subjects come to you, they cannot neglect to offer submission to you, who are their rulers and lords, and those who obtain from you what they wish present themselves to the greatness of your court. And if they have the opportunity to come to the royal house, they cast an admiring glance at its beautiful building, but they offer respect to you as “all in all.”

13.8.8.en: You, O kings, build your palaces and adorn them for yourselves, but the world was not created because God needs it. For God is everything in Himself: light unapproachable, a perfect world, power and mind.

13.8.9.en: If the world is a musical instrument moving in a well measured time, then I worship the Being who gave it this harmony, and played upon it the musical note, and sang its harmonious phrases, and I do not worship the instrument itself.

13.8.10.en: In musical contests the judges do not crown the lyres, ignoring the players upon them...

13.8.11.en: If anyone perceives the various elements of the world as powers of God, we do not approach the powers to offer them submission, but offer it to their Maker and Lord. I do not ask of matter what it cannot give, nor do I pass over God and give honor to the elements, which are unable to do anything other than what was appointed for them.

13.8.12.en: For despite the beauty of their appearance because of the skill of their Creator, they still bear the nature of matter...

13.8.13.en: While I admire the heavens and their elements for their creative design, I do not worship them as gods, knowing that the law of perishing rules over them.

13.9.s.en: 2. The deification of dead human work

13.9.0.en: 10 But miserable are they, and their hope is in dead things, who called them gods, which are the works of men's hands, gold and silver, the inventions of art, and the likenesses of beasts, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. 11 Now a carpenter cuts down a tree from the forest, fit for the work, and skillfully strips off all its bark, and then with good craft makes it into a vessel serviceable for the uses of life, 12 and uses the leavings of his work to dress his food. 13 Then he takes a piece of what is left, which is good for nothing, a crooked piece of wood and full of knots, and carves it with diligence in his idle hours, and shapes it by the skill of his craft into the form of a man, 14 or makes it like some vile beast, smearing it with vermilion, and with paint coloring it red, and covering every stain in it. 15 And he makes for it a fitting place, and sets it in the wall, and fastens it with iron, 16 taking heed that it not fall, knowing that it cannot help itself, for it is an image and has need of help. 17 Then he prays to it concerning his goods and his wives and his children, and is not ashamed to speak to that which has no soul. 18 For health he asks of that which is weak, and for life he entreats that which is dead, and for help he implores that which is utterly unable to help, 19 and for a journey he begs of that which cannot walk, and for gain and trade and success in his undertakings he asks ability of that which is of all things the least able.

13.9.1.en: After speaking of the deification of creation or of some creatures or natural phenomena, he now speaks of the deification of human work, such as idols and statues. In speaking of creation he perhaps found an excuse to offer for them, though this excuse is unacceptable, because they ought to have been occupied with the Creator and not the creation, however great its beauty or power, and it was fitting for them to use their minds that God gave them, and so perceive what is beyond creation. But for man to worship a statue of wood or metal or stone is absurdity and misery.

13.9.2.en: But how miserable are those who set their hope on dead things, and called the works of men's hands gods, gold and silver skillfully made, and images of beasts, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. [10]

13.9.3.en: The folly of man has reached the point that he enslaves himself to what he makes with his own hands, dead things. Goldsmiths and silversmiths, or sculptors, or carpenters, labor skillfully to fashion a dead idol. It is written in the book of Jeremiah the prophet: “For the customs of the people are vain: for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman, with the axe. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it move not. They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:3-5).

13.9.4.en: * God put the knowledge of Himself in human hearts from the beginning. But this knowledge they foolishly poured into wood and stones, and by this they corrupted the truth, at least as far as they were able, while the truth is firm and unchanging, having its unchanging glory.

13.9.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Like a wise physician, before speaking of the disease he pointed to its causes and its source. To prepare for the criticism of their evil, he began by pointing to the sources of their weakness: greed and deceit and corrupt assemblies, showing little by little the things that made them fall into the pit of destruction, when he adds: “the work of their own hands” (Isa 2:8). For what is more absurd than to see a man making a god? Holy Scripture is accustomed to call idols “abominations” (Mt 24:15; Dan 11:31; 12:11).

13.9.6.en: St. John Chrysostom In (Isaiah 44) he spoke of the need of a smith and a carpenter and other skilled workmen to make the idol that the pagans worship.

13.10.0.en: Now a skillful woodcutter saws down a tree easy to handle, and skillfully strips off all its bark, and then with good craft makes it into a vessel serviceable for the uses of life. [11]

13.10.1.en: The skill of carpenters is a gift from God, but in their full freedom they can misuse this gift...

13.10.2.en: It was fitting for the carpenter to use his skill in making household or farming tools, or for sailing, such as ships, and so on, for the benefit of mankind; but to make of them a statue to take the place of the Creator is a crime and a transgression of the divine commandment.

13.10.3.en: * By worshipping things of wood and stone they do not see that, while they trample under foot and burn what in no way differs from them, they call parts of these materials gods. And what they were using in their service a short time before, they carve and worship in their folly, without seeing or thinking at all that they are not worshipping gods but the work of a turner.

13.10.4.en: For as long as the stone is not hewn and the wood is not worked, they tread upon the one and use the other for their various purposes, even in base uses. But when the craftsman fashions them according to his skill, and shapes the material into the form of a man or a woman, then, thanking the craftsman, they begin to worship them as gods, after they had bought them from the turner for a price. And besides this, the maker of images often prays to his own creations, as though he had forgotten the work that he himself finished, and calls gods those which he was cutting and carving and turning a short time before.

13.11.0.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic And uses the leavings of it to dress his food, and is filled. [12]

13.11.1.en: He does not deny the role of the carpenter in making useful wooden tools; even the leavings are used as fuel for cooking food.

13.11.2.en: In Isaiah 44 the prophet portrays for us how they use the wood, part of it for warmth, another for cooking food, and the rest they make into a god, an idol, before which they fall down and worship, and pray to it, saying: “Deliver me; for You are my god” (Isa 44:17).

13.11.3.en: * If it were a god, all the trees would have to be divine. Why then do you use what is left of the wood to obtain a fire that serves you in preparing food...? Do you not put wood in the fire, of the same kind of wood to which you pay worship? How then do you cast away the one and worship the other? Rightly he adds: “They have not known nor understood: for He has shut their eyes, that they cannot see; and their hearts, that they cannot understand. And none considers in his heart, neither is there knowledge nor understanding to say, I have burned part of it in the fire...” (Isa 44:18-19).

13.12.0.en: Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus But a castaway piece that is good for nothing, a crooked piece of wood and full of knots, he takes and carves with diligence in his idle hours, and shapes it with skill that he may gain times of rest, and makes it the form of a man. [13]

13.12.1.en: In some detail he describes how the idol is made; in irony he shows that it is not made even of a precious stone, but of the refuse of trees. As for his saying: “skill that he may gain times of rest,” it means that man, having become inwardly empty, finds nothing useful to practice, and so exercises his craft in fashioning a statue. Truly the inner emptiness is behind atheism!

13.12.2.en: The wise man portrays a carpenter who goes to the forest and chooses a tree or some of its branches, cuts it down, and takes it to his house or his workshop. He divides it into parts and slabs and then strips off the outer covering of the tree, and after using it to make some utensil for the house or for farming, and so on, he looks for a castaway piece, not to use it as fuel, but to make of it a statue that he worships.

13.12.3.en: Here he alludes to the vanity of emperors and kings, who make statues of themselves that men may worship them in their lifetime and after their death; by this they think that they exercise lordship over the people even after their death. At the same time some simple people in their weakness think that their lives are in the hands of these mighty ones even after their death.

13.12.4.en: In contempt of idolaters the author shows that an idol can be made from the refuse of wood, and in this there is shame!

13.12.5.en: * He says (Isa 44:13) that he copies (for the idol) not divine but human features, and forms a human image and worships his own image as a god. Then the prophet Isaiah teaches us (Isa 44:14) that the forests that are on the mountains were given by the Creator to men, that they might be permitted to use them to kindle fire and serve the needs of their bodies. But these, on the contrary, take evergreen branches, or an oak, or a pine tree, which the God of the universe planted and supplied with rain for the benefit of man and to provide him with many material goods, yet they use them to make gods.

13.13.0.en: Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus Or makes it like some vile beast, smearing it with crimson, and with paint coloring its surface red, and covering every blemish in it. [14]

13.13.1.en: What adds to the absurdity of the matter is that the carpenter makes a statue not of an emperor or a king but of an animal or some trivial insect, and shows skill in carving and forming the statue, and man falls down before it and worships it, and offers it sacrifices and offerings.

13.13.2.en: They saw in birds and animals certain symbols. The falcon and the eagle are known for sharpness of sight, so they symbolized wisdom and far-sightedness. The calf symbolizes fertility, and the serpent life, since it changes its skin from time to time.

13.14.0.en: And makes for it a shrine fitting for it, and sets it in the wall, and fastens it with iron. [15]

13.14.1.en: In a new contempt he mocks those who busy themselves with making shrines fastened with nails on the wall in order that the statues may be kept in them lest they fall and be broken. For the statue is unable to bear itself, so the nails bear it.

13.14.2.en: The author mocks the place or dwelling that is fastened with iron on a wall for the idol to be put in it.

13.14.3.en: By his saying: “fitting for it” he mocks the statue, for which nothing is fitting except to be set as upon a wall, having no work and no power to move.

13.15.0.en: Taking care lest it fall, knowing that it cannot help itself, for it is an image and has need of help! [16]

13.15.1.en: A statue that needs iron nails to fasten it or its shrine in the wall, and whose owner fears its falling, how can it raise up those who fall?

13.15.2.en: The wise man exposes the weakness of the pagan gods: they are unable to help themselves, so how can they help those who worship them? These dead gods, how can they give life to others, and being unable to move, how can they support man in his movements and his journeys?

13.15.3.en: Holy Scripture in both its Testaments, as well as church history through the ages down to our present day, has shown us how God desires to restore man to his first dominion in the Garden of Eden.

13.15.4.en: We give a few examples here:

13.15.5.en: God gave Joshua the son of Nun authority to stop the motion of some of the heavenly bodies, that the day might be lengthened and he might gain victory over the wicked who resisted the divine truth (Josh 10).

13.15.6.en: God gave Elijah the prophet authority, so that he brought down fire that consumed the captains of fifty and their men, because they were arrogant against God Himself in the person of His prophet (2 Kgs 1:10), and also he asked for fire from heaven to consume a sacrifice, to bring the people back to the true knowledge of God (1 Kgs 18:38). As He gave him.

13.15.7.en: God gave many of the saints authority over nature and wild animals, but within limits lest they fall into pride. Among these was St. Anasimon, with whom lions made friends.

13.15.8.en: * O what dangerous folly! What kind of gods are these gods of yours, which can be stolen? Are you not ashamed to say: “Why did you steal them?”

13.16.0.en: St. John Chrysostom And when he wants to pray for his goods and his marriage and his children, he is not ashamed to address that which has no soul, and for health he implores that which is weak. [17]

13.16.1.en: God looks upon men for whose sake He created the world with all its possibilities and beauty, and sees them asking a piece of wood to support them in the management of their money or their married life or their children or for their healing, while this statue is lifeless, having no life in it, and unable even to move.

13.16.2.en: In amazement the author mocks him who asks health of an idol in which there is no life, and asks strength of what has no strength, and asks help of what has no experience, and asks protection on his journeys of an idol unable to move.

13.17.0.en: And for life he entreats that which is dead, and for help he implores that which has no experience at all, and for a successful journey, that which cannot take a step. [18]

13.17.1.en: * What is more absurd than these men? Though they have been given a mind, and enjoy wonderful privileges from the compassions of God, they worship a lifeless stone, and are far from being ashamed or feeling any absurdity. They deal with it as with dumb beasts. Therefore Paul also wrote these words: “You know that you were Gentiles, carried away to these dumb idols, even as you were led” (1 Cor 12:2). Rightly he said: “dumb”; people who have the gift of speech, who enjoy reason and hearing, resort to things that have not these qualities, but resemble dumb animals. What excuse can such men have?

13.18.0.en: St. John Chrysostom And for gain and enterprise and the success of his hands' work, he seeks strength of that which has no strength in its hands. [19]

13.18.1.en: The man who has died through sin needs One who is able to raise him from death; he who is exposed to troubles from satanic wars and sicknesses and afflictions needs One who lifts him above pain and brings him across to the blessed life; he who walks through life as on a passing journey needs One able to lift him to heaven; and he who needs strength for work and ability to think in order to succeed needs that Almighty One who gives strength. Who is able to give all this to man except the incarnate Word of God and His heavenly wisdom! How can man exchange this heavenly One who loves mankind for a dead statue unable to lead itself?!

13.18.2.en: * “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it has no stalk; the bud shall yield no meal” (Hos 8:7)... there is no fruit to gather as your harvest from the service of the idol; as for their sheaves, they are like ears of wheat shattered by the wind: many stalks appear outwardly, but there is not a single seed in them. Such is the nature of idolatry: on one side it can take the form of a man or a woman, or a lion or any other animal through art (sculpture), and on the other side it is deprived of any power or energy.

13.19.0.en: Isaiah chapter 44 gives us a wonderful picture of the corruption of idol worship, showing that the idols and their makers and those who worship them all bear shame and vanity. The makers of idols are earnest, regarding neither hunger nor thirst nor weariness (Isa 44:12), as they make the axe from iron and beat out plates to set up statues. So also with the carpenters, who spend every effort to carve wooden statues. All of them toil and do not tire to set up metal or wooden statues unable to give salvation, while the children of God are lax in their spiritual striving, though they enjoy divine possibilities able to bring them to the enjoyment of eternal salvation. It is as though these laborers in vain condemn the lax children of God, as the Lord of glory Jesus said that the children of this generation are wiser than the children of the Kingdom (Lk 16:8).

13.19.1.en: On another side, making metal statues exhausts the energy of the workmen, while making wooden statues is accompanied by amusement with what is left over of the wood, since it is used in the hearth for warmth or for cooking food, at the very time in which they quiet their conscience by worshipping the wood carved into a statue.

13.19.2.en: Finally, what does the worship of idols (or withdrawal from God) offer:

13.19.3.en: a- Blindness of inner insight and inner darkness (Isa 44:18), while Christ is the Sun of Righteousness (Mal 4:2).

13.19.4.en: b- Ignorance and lack of knowledge (Isa 44:19), while Christ is our righteousness.

13.19.5.en: c- Hunger, so that man eats ashes (Isa 44:20), while the Lord Christ is the heavenly bread.

13.19.6.en: d- Lying and deceit and misleading (Isa 44:20), while the Lord Christ is the Way and the Truth.

13.19.7.en: In other words, we find in our Christ inner enlightenment, knowledge, satisfaction, truth and all our needs, but outside Him there is nothing but inner emptiness, a feeling of isolation and loss of inner insight.

13.19.8.en: * He shows (Isa 44:12-13) that the forming of what are called gods depends on many resources. For their maker needs a smith to prepare the tools and a grinder to make the tools sharp. And on his part, as a skilled craftsman, he needs coal and fire to help him. Besides this, the maker of these things experiences the desire to eat and drink. All these successive things are necessary to make a god for fools to worship.

13.19.11.en: * My soul thirsts for the good, and will keep praising You for the abundance of Your generosity.

13.19.12.en: All that is around me bears witness to Your love for me, and Your surpassing care.

13.19.13.en: You gave me this beautiful world; You offered me every possibility of a happy life.

13.19.14.en: You have not withheld from me anything of the works of Your honor.

13.19.15.en: The earth and the oceans and the firmament and space and all the planets cry out, speaking to me in the language of creation about You, O heavenly Artist!

13.19.16.en: The voice of nature does not leave my ear!

13.19.17.en: Glory to You, my wonderful Creator!

13.19.18.en: * In folly my fathers worshipped the creation and not its Creator.

13.19.19.en: They turned their backs to You, and deified what You gave them.

13.19.20.en: They worshipped the gift, not the Giver!

13.19.21.en: The beauty and power of the work of Your hands dazzled them; instead of praising You, they praised perishing beings!

13.19.22.en: Why should I lay the blame on my fathers, when I complain of myself to You.

13.19.23.en: Often I have enslaved myself to what You gave me; instead of ruling over temporal things, I became by my own will a slave to them.

13.19.24.en: It ruled me instead of my ruling it.

13.19.25.en: It moves me like a toy in its hands, instead of my moving it for the edification of my soul.

13.19.26.en: Restore to me my freedom and my dignity, and the wisdom that You gave me.

13.19.27.en: * How can I worship what has no life, and leave You, O eternal Life?

13.19.28.en: You are the Creator of all and the Giver of life.

13.19.29.en: Let me possess You, for You are the Supreme Good.

13.19.30.en: You are the Giver of authority and freedom.

13.19.31.en: You are the One who satisfies soul and body together!

13.19.33.en: * Enter the door of my heart, so that no other has a place in it.

13.19.34.en: Occupy it, and establish Your kingdom within it.

13.19.35.en: Declare Your glory and Your authority in me.

13.19.36.en: Enter and dwell in it, that I may abide in You.

13.19.37.en: Rest within me, that I may rest in Your divine bosom!

13.19.38.en: * My God, my soul has no bridegroom but You!

13.19.39.en: I have no strength except in You.

13.19.40.en: I have no incorruption except by union with You.

13.19.41.en: I have no gain except by possessing You!

13.19.42.en: Let me worship You with all my being: let my body glorify You, and my soul praise You, and my will, which You have sanctified, sing to You!

13.19.43.en: Finally I cry to You, hasten and come, O Beloved of my soul, for my heart shall not cling to the love of the world.

13.19.44.en: It awaits its swift passage to You.

13.19.45.en: Come to me, and I will come to You by Your Holy Spirit!
